articles.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes a day before U.S.-brokered talks are scheduled to begin
articles.summary: President Donald Trump mentioned in a "60 Minutes" interview that the two sides are "very close" to a deal.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia battered Ukraine's power grid again and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia's biggest oil refineries, officials said Monday, hours before delegations from Moscow and Kyiv were due to meet for new U.S.-brokered talks on how to end the fighting. Nearly five years after Russia invaded its neighbor, the two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say. The three-way talks between envoys from the U.S., Russia and Ukraine are due to start in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and last for two days. The previous round of talks was in February. U.S. President Donald Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv are "very close" to a deal, despite the "tremendous hatred" between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said that Ukraine would have "a little bit different shape" under the settlement, but he didn't elaborate. Trump has previously made statements about developments in the war which haven't materialized. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who will mediate in the talks with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, said that the priorities will be ending the conflict, finding ways to stop the war reigniting, reviving Ukraine's postwar economy and preparing humanitarian aid. "We hope these discussions will identify areas of common ground, advance practical solutions, and build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations," Kushner said on X Monday. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday that Trump's team has placed "collective security," covering not just Russia and Ukraine but also a wider area, at the top of the agenda. The last three-way talks, in Geneva nine months ago, also took place amid continuing attacks. They delivered no significant progress in ending the war, but some circumstances have changed. Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, has to reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections. They could demand more support for Ukraine. Russian state finances are under heavy strain because of the war, and Ukraine's economy is being choked by the relentless attacks. In Abu Dhabi, the talks will look at what security guarantees would satisfy Russia, which sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine, which wants to prevent future Russian invasions. Putin has sought to sideline European countries and negotiate Ukraine's future directly with Trump. However, European leaders and Ukraine have insisted that they be included. Moscow says that European representatives won't be directly involved in the Abu Dhabi discussions, but European officials said that representatives will be in the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine's lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, said that European officials will hold "separate coordination" with the delegation from Kyiv. Kushner said that before the talks in Abu Dhabi begin, he and Witkoff will consult with officials from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that the meeting would focus on trilateral negotiations, with the United States mediating between Russia and Ukraine. "You are aware that the Americans have their own channels of communication with the Europeans, as do the Ukrainians, and it appears they are already establishing their own methods of coordination," Peskov said. "But, to reiterate, this is a matter of trilateral negotiations." Russian forces targeted four electrical substations in Ukraine's Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, Russia's Defense Ministry said Monday. The attacks are part of Russia's campaign to deny Ukrainian civilians heating, light and running water during the approaching winter. Zelenskyy said Monday that the European Union had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power grid repairs. Russia launched 317 drones of various types including 105 jet-powered drones at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said. Russian aerial attacks have pummeled Ukraine throughout the war, with gruesome consequences. A Russian glide bomb attack last week near the front line in the southern Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 55 people at an aid distribution center. On Monday, Russian forces hit a warehouse in Odesa in southwestern Ukraine containing food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said. Meanwhile, an attack by long-range drones developed by Ukraine during the war started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, close to St. Petersburg and more than 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from the Ukrainian border, Leningrad Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said Monday. Ukraine said in early October that its long-range strikes had neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces. Ukrainian forces also struck a plant near St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, that produces solid rocket propellant for Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Ukraine's General Staff said. Ukraine is trying to prevent Russia from firing ballistic missiles, which Kyiv's forces can't stop once they are in the air without more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems. Patriot missiles, however, are in short supply.

articles.title: Republican congressman launches impeachment procedure against US defence chief Hegseth
articles.summary: Republican Kentucky Congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, including alleged violations of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, as well as misconduct involving civilian casualties and operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
articles.body: Days after US President Donald Trump's party suffered a drastic midterm defeat, a Republican lawmaker has made a move to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives as early as this week.Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has submitted on Monday eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abusing his powers and illegally waging war on Iran.He also cited the school attack launched in the early days of the war that began in late February, in which a US strike killed 120 children.Massie is using a special procedure that requires the House to consider his resolution within two days, meaning the vote could take place as early as Wednesday in the currently Republican-controlled House, with some lawmakers potentially joining Democrats in backing the charges.Hegseth had "knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders" by waging war without congressional approval, Massie said on the House floor.Trump continues to give unwavering support to HegsethAlthough impeachment would be a humiliating blow to the Trump administration, the US president continued to back Hegseth on Monday, saying he would stand by him if he were impeached.Trump said that Hegseth had done a "good job" and had "won" wars in Iran and Venezuela, referring to the illegal capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.Even if Hegseth is impeached, he would not automatically be removed from office, as conviction and removal would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate, a much tougher hurdle, even after Democrats take control on 3 January.The Republicans' recent election defeat has caused divisions within the party, potentially leading some lawmakers to abstain from voting and making it easier for the impeachment resolution to pass.

Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
articles.body: "He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched. Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations. Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang. According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia. Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage. Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday. The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team. Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns. Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy. The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China." At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. "I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added. He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy". Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities. The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear. A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang". Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees. Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company. Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent. It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions. Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market. What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows
articles.summary: Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.
articles.body: Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz . Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change . While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026. "It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway. The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference . The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%. "A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%." It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered. While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves. "The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University. And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

articles.title: Moldovan foreign affairs minister says constitutional neutrality must not be impediment to strengthening country’s defense capabilities
articles.summary: Moldovan foreign affairs minister says constitutional neutrality must not be impediment to strengthening country’s defense capabilities The constitutional neutrality must not be an impediment to strengthening the country’s defense capabilities. Moldova must make use of opportunities for cooperation with the European Union in the field of security.
articles.body: Moldovan foreign affairs minister says constitutional neutrality must not be impediment to strengthening country’s defense capabilities The constitutional neutrality must not be an impediment to strengthening the country’s defense capabilities. Moldova must make use of opportunities for cooperation with the European Union in the field of security. In recent years, the support provided through the European Peace Facility (EPF) has increased from 7 million euros in 2021 to 120 million euros in 2026. Deputy Prime Minister, Foreign Affairs Minister Mihai Popsoi has made statements to this effect during the annual conference on European Union enlargement, held today in Chisinau. According to the official, in recent years, the EPF has provided transformational support to the security and defense sector. “The amounts granted are colossal for the defense budget of Moldova, a sector that was neglected for decades. Given the horrors Ukraine has been going through for almost five years and their repercussions on the entire region, we must understand that a neutral country must invest more in its own defense than other states that have the peace, security and luxury of belonging to a collective defense alliance. Within the great European family, security cooperation, the strengthening of the defense industry and the development of logistical networks are mechanisms that Moldova wants to be part of. We must understand that neutrality does not mean being incapable of defending yourself. Nor does it represent an obstacle to strengthening defense capabilities and making investments in the field of defense, which we are making and will continue to make,” Mihai Popsoi said. The minister emphasized that, in addition to the EPF, the European Union also supported programmes in the civilian sector, which play an important role in strengthening societal security. “I am referring to the European Union Partnership Mission in Moldova. This mission has helped us enormously to strengthen our capabilities in the field of information security and crisis management. The Crisis Management Center and the strengthening of its capabilities are part of our accession commitments. Therefore, the existing cooperation mechanism, which is continuously developing, represents a major opportunity for Moldova to strengthen its defense and security sector, as well as society’s resilience as a whole. A state can succeed, only if every citizen and institution contributes to defending society against foreign interference. Our citizens have become aware of the danger to which we are exposed and, every time, we have proved our ability to defend our democratic choices, our right to choose our own destiny and to continue efforts to enhance the resilience of our society. This undoubtedly demonstrates our internal capacity to respond to these challenges, but it is also the result of substantial EU support,” Mihai Popsoi added. For his part, Stanislav Secrieru, the president’s chief adviser on defense and national security, noted that, under the UN Charter, every independent and sovereign state has the right to self-defense; however, in order to exercise this right, it must have the necessary means. “At present, we notice that, in the European Union, some states are investing in defense and increasing their military budgets. At the same time, neutral countries also contribute to the EPF, from which Moldova benefits through defense resources. Therefore, being neutral does not mean being passive, indifferent or failing to take care of one’s own defense capabilities. Threats in the air domain are evolving every two or three weeks. Modernizing airspace surveillance capabilities is a lengthy process, as drones flying at low altitudes require specialized radars. Moreover, even if Moldova had the financial resources, the delivery of equipment would not be immediate, as manufacturers are prioritizing orders for Ukraine, where the situation is more serious. Another challenge concerns training and retaining in service specialists capable of operating increasingly sophisticated equipment,” Stanislav Secrieru said. A 120-million-euros-worth assistance package is being provided by the European Union through the European Peace Facility (EPF) and is meant to strengthen the country’s defense capabilities. Moldova is the second-largest beneficiary of EU assistance provided through the EPF, after Ukraine. Thus, the total support provided to the country amounts to 317 million euros for the period 2021–2026. articles.title: Constitutional Court only partially grants Lelo's motion regarding examination of evidence during hearing
articles.summary: The Plenum of the Constitutional Court has only partially granted the motion filed by the political union of citizens Lelo – Strong Georgia regarding the examination of evidence during the hearing. The decision was communicated to the parties by the Chairman of the Constitutional Court, Revaz Nadaraia.
articles.body: The Plenum of the Constitutional Court has only partially granted the motion filed by the political union of citizens Lelo – Strong Georgia regarding the examination of evidence during the hearing. The decision was communicated to the parties by the Chairman of the Constitutional Court, Revaz Nadaraia. "The motion filed by the respondent party—the political union of citizens 'Lelo – Strong Georgia'—has been granted in part. The request to present every single internet link cited in the constitutional claim during the court proceedings is denied. Furthermore, the Court will not examine—during the hearing on the merits—facts that are 'generally known' (as per Article 31 of the Constitutional Court’s Regulations) or judicial acts that have already entered into legal force. During the course of the proceedings, the Court will assess the relevance of specific pieces of evidence cited in the claim—should their relevance be contested—either upon a substantiated motion from a party or on its own initiative. The ruling is final and is not subject to review or appeal. The Plenum was unanimous in adopting this ruling," stated Revaz Nadaraia. For context, "Lelo – Strong Georgia" had requested that an evidentiary hearing stage be conducted during the Constitutional Court’s proceedings regarding the lawsuit filed by "Georgian Dream" MPs, which seeks the banning of five opposition parties. This motion was submitted by Levan Samushia, representing the respondent side; however, representatives of other opposition parties also expressed their support for it.

articles.title: Hearings resume at Constitutional Court regarding potential ban of five opposition parties
articles.summary: The Constitutional Court has resumed hearings on a petition filed by Georgian Dream MPs seeking the banning of five opposition parties. The phase of the proceedings dedicated to opening statements and explanations has concluded; starting today, the Constitutional Court is moving on to the questioning stage.
articles.body: The Constitutional Court has resumed hearings on a petition filed by Georgian Dream MPs seeking the banning of five opposition parties. The phase of the proceedings dedicated to opening statements and explanations has concluded; starting today, the Constitutional Court is moving on to the questioning stage. As explained by the Chairman of the Constitutional Court, Revaz Nadaraia, the Court will first pose questions to the plaintiffs, followed by the respondents. For context, the Constitutional Court began reviewing the petition on October 21. The case is being heard by a plenum consisting of seven judges of the Constitutional Court. The petition submitted to the Constitutional Court is signed by 88 Members of Parliament. Based on their lawsuit, the court is set to consider the issue of declaring the following five political associations unconstitutional: "Unity – National Movement"; "Coalition for Change – Gvaramia, Melia, Girchi, Droa"; "Strong Georgia – Lelo, For the People, For Freedom!"; the "Federalist Party"; and the party "Gakharia for Georgia." The constitutional lawsuit is accompanied by the conclusion of a temporary investigative commission established within the 11th convocation of the Parliament.

articles.title: Constitutional Court to resume consideration of Georgian Dream petition seeking the banning of five opposition parties
articles.summary: The Constitutional Court will resume hearings today regarding a petition filed by Georgian Dream MPs seeking the ban of five opposition parties. Additionally, further hearings related to this petition are scheduled for November 11, 12, and 13, starting at 11:00 AM.
articles.body: The Constitutional Court will resume hearings today regarding a petition filed by Georgian Dream MPs seeking the ban of five opposition parties. Additionally, further hearings related to this petition are scheduled for November 11, 12, and 13, starting at 11:00 AM. The Constitutional Court is currently conducting a substantive review of a case initiated by 88 "Georgian Dream" members of the Parliament of Georgia. The petition concerns the constitutionality of the activities of several political parties—"Unity – National Movement," "Coalition for Change (Gvaramia, Melia, Girchi, Droa)," "Strong Georgia (Lelo, For the People, For Freedom!)," the "Federalist Party," and "Gakharia – For Georgia"—and seeks their prohibition. A session previously scheduled for November 9 was postponed due to the health condition of one of the judges.

IRGC unveils new missile city
articles.summary: The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force unveiled a new missile city, displaying various ballistic and cruise missiles along with their launchers, Tasnim News Agency reports. The unveiling ceremony was attended by Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces Major General Ali Abdollahi and Commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force Brigadier General Majid Mousavi.
articles.body: The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force unveiled a new missile city, displaying various ballistic and cruise missiles along with their launchers, Tasnim News Agency reports. The unveiling ceremony was attended by Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces Major General Ali Abdollahi and Commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force Brigadier General Majid Mousavi. A range of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as their launch systems, were put on display at the facility. The unveiling follows an announcement by IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi that the Aerospace Force would introduce a new underground missile city and several other military achievements during the IRGC Aerospace Force Week. Mohebbi said the force had rapidly moved its missile and drone production lines from surface facilities to underground sites, going beyond underground storage complexes to establish “missile production cities” deep beneath the ground. He said Iran’s domestic expertise, vast territory and flexible production infrastructure would ensure that weapons manufacturing could continue even under heavy bombardment.

articles.body: The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja). The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward. Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes. Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.

articles.title: Oil price relief as Trump declares US war on Iran ‘ending fairly soon’ | First Thing
articles.summary: Speaking in the White House, the president said the US remained ‘locked and loaded’ but escalation was not needed. Plus how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus Good morning.
articles.body: Good morning. Oil prices have dropped after Donald Trump unilaterally declared that the US war on Iran was “effectively over” . During a White House press conference, Trump said Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and that an escalation was not needed. He said, however, that the US remained “locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason”, adding: “We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon.” Brent crude has dropped below $90, its lowest level since August . What is the latest development with Pete Hegseth? A Republican lawmaker has moved to force a vote to impeach the US defense secretary . Thomas Massie, of Kentucky, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers. What has happened at a US airbase in England? The US military has reportedly evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in ⁠Britain after a threat from Iran. Two US refuelling tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base diverted to Germany on Monday morning, while several other tankers at the base ⁠were moved to Germany and other locations later in the day. Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, have been accused of defrauding shareholders in a lawsuit over the Chinese spying scandal engulfing the $4.3tn company. The legal action came as Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. There is little public information available about Alice Huang, a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is an intelligence asset. Rebecca Bailey has put together what we know about her , while Aisha Down and Dan Milmo have this exploration of how the affair may have harmed US security . The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue his administration’s construction of a border wall in Texas’s Big Bend region, including parts of Big Bend national park. The nation’s highest court granted the Trump administration’s emergency request to suspend a lower court order that had temporarily stopped the project. Opponents have argued the project threatens wildlife and public lands, and could destroy “iconic sections” of the Rio Grande’s protected river corridor. A Massachusetts judge cleared the way for Lindsay Clancy to be tried again on ⁠murder charges for killing her three young children, saying a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to a ⁠double prosecution for the same ⁠crime. He rejected an attempt by Clancy’s attorneys to have the case against her dismissed. In September the judge declared ⁠a mistrial after the jury reported that a holdout juror was preventing it from reaching a unanimous verdict. March has been floated as the timing for a second trial. The disgraced actor and comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced in London to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. Brand – who has recently tried to reinvent himself as a Christian influencer and has been a featured speaker for a Maha group allied with RFK Jr – was described by the British judge as a sexual predator who had used his fame and power to carry out crimes and protect himself. M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything , a post-apocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast in England. The 81-year-old becomes the oldest winner in the award’s history, and the first science fiction author to win it. France has said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind “unprecedented” cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month. An Ohio State fraternity has been suspended after a viral video showed two men on fire. The university and police are conducting investigations over the “extremely concerning incident”. California voters failed to pass a proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth. Joe Biden will undertake only limited promotion of his upcoming White House memoir because of advancing cancer , the former president has said. articles.summary: Seventeen years after the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Bosnia’s constitution unlawfully discriminates against Roma, Jews and 15 other minorities, they remain barred from the country’s highest political offices.
articles.body: In Sarajevo, the election campaign posters hang from lampposts, walls, fences and billboards. To the uninitiated, it is a jungle. At junctions, there are several, or even a dozen or so at a time: small posters, larger ones, huge billboards. Smiling men, a few women. Surnames, numbers, parties, nations. You need to know who’s who to make sense of this jigsaw puzzle. The October 4 general elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina involved several levels of government all at once. Depending on where they live, voters chose representatives for the three-person Presidency, the state House of Representatives, the parliaments of both parts of the country – the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation – and the cantonal assemblies within the Federation. But these elections were about more than simply filling a few thousand positions across several levels of government. The elections took place in the wake of one of Bosnia's most turbulent political periods in recent years. Milorad Dodik, for years the most powerful politician in Republika Srpska, lost his office as its president in 2025 following a final court ruling. His SNSD party, however, remained one of the country’s main political forces. Prior to this, the ruling coalition at state level had collapsed, and a new majority had failed to materialise. Furthermore, Bosnia conducts its politics with Serbia on one side, Croatia on the other, and within its borders two parts of the state and three constituent nations, whose parties still largely run separate campaigns. International election observers describe a deeply fragmented political landscape, with campaign narratives still rooted in wartime divisions. The SNSD speaks of defending Republika Srpska, Croatian parties of political representation for Croats, and Bosniak parties, amongst other things, of strengthening the state and the position of Bosniaks. In Bosnia, therefore, elections still very often begin with the question: who will represent ‘our people’? These elections brought technological changes, too. Biometric identification and ballot scanners were introduced across the country, intended to make voting more secure and increase confidence in the process. International observers subsequently reported genuine electoral competition, but also technical difficulties and problems with ballot secrecy. The EU welcomed the new technology while acknowledging shortcomings in its implementation. So, Bosnia is changing the way it counts votes. Changing the rules governing who can stand for high office is proving much harder. I walk through Sarajevo, looking at all the faces staring back at me, and think of one person who is not on those posters: Dervo Sejdic. The Bosnian constitution was drawn up as part of the Dayton Agreement, which in 1995 brought an end to the brutal wars in the Balkans. Peace had to be forged between the three warring parties, so the state was built around three ‘constituent peoples’: Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats. The system was designed to end a war, not to create an ideal democracy. But what helped secure peace in 1995 has, over the decades, also helped entrench the very ethnic divisions it was meant to contain. Thirty-one years later, those divisions still shape the political life of this small country. To put it simply: at the highest levels of government, the chairs are labelled with the names of the nations. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina has three seats: one for a Bosniak, one for a Croat and one for a Serb. The 15 seats in the state’s House of Peoples are also divided between these three groups: 3 times 5 equals 15. If you are a Romani person, a Jew or do not wish to identify as any of the three nations, you cannot stand for election to these positions. You can vote, you can become a councillor, you can work in the civil service, you can pay taxes. But you will never become president. Never. By design. In 2006, Dervo Sejdic, Romani, and Jakob Finci, Jewish, lodged complaints with the European Court of Human Rights, or ECHR. Three years later, they won their case. The Grand Chamber of the court ruled that such exclusion constituted blatant discrimination and should be rectified. That was in December 2009. Since then, Bosnia has held another election. And another. And another. Yet the constitutional seats still bear the same labels. The year after he won his case against his own country in Strasbourg, Sejdic wrote to Bosnia’s Central Electoral Commission. He knew the judgement had not yet been implemented, but he thought he would ask anyway: could he, in the spirit of that judgement, stand as a candidate for the Presidency? The reply, as he recalls it today, went something like this: “You may come; you may submit your documents. The Constitution and the Electoral Code will give you the answer.” In short: no. Seventeen years later, I ask him: “If the ruling had been carried out back then, perhaps your face would be on those posters today. Do you ever think about that?” “All the time,” he says. “Why should I be any worse than other presidential candidates?” Sejdic’s case shows you can succeed before the ECHR yet, 17 years later, still be unable to exercise the right you fought for and won. The court cannot walk into the Bosnian parliament and amend the constitution. Bosnia and Herzegovina is obliged to implement its judgment, and implementation is overseen by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. The Sejdic-Finci case has therefore been returning to the Committee of Ministers for years. I asked the Council of Europe what exactly 17 years of waiting means. The reply leaves little room for diplomatic interpretation: “The continued retention of the present discriminatory electoral system constitutes a clear violation of the requirements of the European Convention on Human Rights, going to the heart of the democratic process.” The Committee of Ministers, which supervises the implementation of the ECHR’s judgments, has set June 2027 for its next examination of the case. If there is no tangible progress by then, it will consider further action. The European Commission also insists that the issue remains on its agenda. “The EU has underlined the importance of implementing the Sejdic-Finci case law since the 2009 judgement of the European Court of Human Rights,” a Commission spokesperson tells BIRN. Brussels expects reforms ensuring that state institutions function without discrimination as part of Bosnia’s EU accession negotiations, it says. The constitutional changes, however, remain Bosnia’s responsibility. In the meantime, I’m trying to understand who, exactly, can become a European here? Not in a geographical sense, because the geography is simple: Bosnia and Herzegovina lies in Europe. In 2016, it applied for EU membership; in 2022, it was granted candidate status; and in March 2024, the European Council decided to open accession negotiations. Though by the end of September, just before the latest round of elections, the negotiating framework had still not been adopted and the actual negotiations had not yet begun. What interests me, however, is a Europe smaller than the continent and larger than the Union: Europe as the promise that a citizen is a citizen. And this is where the Bosnian problem begins. Because here, one can be a citizen whilst at the same time belong to a category which the constitution refers to as ‘others’, who include, as well as Roma and Jews, 15 other ethnic groups, such as Hungarians, Austrians or Poles. Almir has strong facial features, a shaved head, a thin moustache and a small, neatly trimmed goatee. He wears an immaculate white turtleneck and strong perfume. There’s something of the angry young man about him: he speaks quickly, sharply, sometimes blurting out sentences as if they’d been waiting a long time for their turn. But his anger is well organised. Almir doesn’t just get angry. He breaks things down into their constituent parts, looks for the mechanism behind them, wants to know where they came from. He was seven years old when a few boys shoved him into the boot of a car. Because he was Roma. Only seven-year-old Almir didn’t really understand what that meant yet. He liked drawing. He knew his colours: red, green, brown. When he was doing his homework after that incident, he drew a picture of himself with a brown face. That was all he understood. That was how he could explain to himself what had happened to him: he’s brown – he ends up in the boot. It was only later that his mother explained to him that they were Roma. And that not everyone likes Roma people. Years later, Almir – now a poet, artist and activist – was tidying his flat. His mother had kept his childhood drawings. He found this one too. He looked at the brown face of his seven-year-old self. “I thought: what the fuck?” he says. This, amongst other things, later gave rise to the exhibition “U Sarajevu sve po starom” (Everything’s the same in Sarajevo). Almir began rummaging through the archives. Together with other researchers, he delved further and further back into the history of the media. They found old texts about “Gypsies”, tales of cursed people, and pseudoscientific measurements of skulls. Then they returned to the contemporary media. The words have changed a little. The mechanism – far less so. “Today, you can write ‘Rom’ correctly and then construct a sentence exactly the same way as a hundred years ago,” he explains. “A Rom committed a crime, a Rom caused trouble, a Rom man did something, even though his background is completely irrelevant to the story.” Almir says that hatred is the fuel: “They – the politicians – need hatred to function.” After one of his radio programs, he read the comments posted under his appearance. He was inundated with a wave of hatred, including death threats. I ask Almir when Roma people in Bosnia are truly treated as equals. “Erm… perhaps when they pay their taxes?” he laughs. “Obligations are equal. Rights – rarely.” He also says something that I’ve heard in various forms during my journey through Bosnia during this election season: decisions about the Roma are still too often made by people who aren’t Roma themselves. “The biggest problem is that people who aren’t Roma work on and make decisions about Roma issues, and they think they know everything. But they don’t. Help? A food parcel? Give me a job!” he says. According to Almir, the Roma themselves know best what they need. But here, this angry young man in a white turtleneck starts to contradict himself. Because he definitely doesn’t want to go into politics, even though many people I speak to about him would very much like him to. Almir claims that a political party means immediate division: one group will help you, whilst the rest will try to hinder you. As an artist, he prefers to be independent. But he wants the Roma to be where decisions are made. Which is exactly where he himself doesn’t want to go. Nedzad Jusic is sitting in a restaurant in Tuzla, surrounded by his team: five well-built blokes. I joke that they look like bodyguards. “I would be lost without them!” he replies. He’s been a city councillor in Tuzla for 12 years: “I know the power of decision-making.” There used to be 31 councillors on the council: 15 votes on one side, 15 on the other. Nedzad, a Romani man, held the 31st seat. “It was the Romani vote that made the difference!” he says proudly. But his story began earlier. His father, born in the 1930s, finished school and in 1969 became head of the Red Cross in Tuzla. His mother, a Romani woman, also finished school, at a time when perhaps only half of all girls in the whole country were completing their education. It was she who insisted on her children’s education. Nedzad speaks of her as the driving force behind the family: her sisters and brothers were educated, followed by the next generation. The proof is sitting at the table: the example is passed from hand to hand almost as readily as a bottle of rakija . A father shows his son. A sister shows her brother. An uncle shows his nephew. A policeman shows his daughter. Admir Bibinovic works in the police’s criminal investigation department. He is one of only five Romani police officers in the country. At first, I thought I’d misheard. I ask him: ‘When did you ever feel equal?’ ‘Never.’ He doesn’t answer dramatically, he doesn’t pause for effect. He has never felt equal. He went to the police academy partly thanks to a training course during which someone encouraged him to reflect on his own abilities and talents. He also had role models close to him: his uncle Nedzad and his sister. Now he wants to be a role model for his daughter himself. I ask Nedzad whether a Romani president of Bosnia would make any difference. I expect an answer about setting a symbolic example for young people. ‘Nothing,’ he says. He isn’t interested in symbolism. He’s interested in the ability to make decisions. That’s an important distinction. Because it’s easy, from the outside, to come up with a beautiful story: a Romani child looks at a Romani president and realises for the first time that they can become anything. Nedzad brings me back down to earth. He says that all his life he’s had to work five times as hard to prove he’s just as good as a non-Roma colleague. He wants Roma people where decisions are made, but not because they look good on a poster. It’s about hand number 31. Twenty minutes from this table, there’s another answer to the question of representation. Kiseljak, near Tuzla. Rubbish lies wherever it’s no longer needed: by the roadside, under a fence, between houses. The locals say there isn’t even a communal rubbish container. Lake Modrac is nearby. Tourists used to come here, they say. Now part of the lake has dried up, and mosquitoes swarm over the area. The landscape looks a bit like a promise that nobody has formally revoked, but which has simply ceased to be fulfilled over ti

articles.summary: Russian Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky leads the Russian delegation
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 10. /TASS/. The Russian delegation, which is currently participating in trilateral negotiations with the United States and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, will decide whether to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in a "telegraphic" mode or provide a comprehensive report, depending on how the talks proceed, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday. "The delegation will be making decisions depending on how the negotiations proceed," Peskov said at a news briefing. Talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine on a Ukrainian settlement are held on November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi. Russian Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky leads the Russian delegation, while Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov heads Ukraine’s team. Kremlin Spokesman Peskov stated earlier the negotiations would focus on security guarantees. The two-day talks began on Tuesday at about 8:15 a.m. GMT. The Russian and Ukrainian delegations are seated opposite each other at a U-shaped table.
